localpsidR

Source: readme.md

localpsidR builds long-format panel data sets (one row per person and wave) from Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) raw data. It is a fork of psidR by Florian Oswald, and the original authors keep full credit for the package.

Installation

remotes::install_github("jgonzhijon/localpsidR")

install.packages("psidR") installs the original package, not this fork.

Data requirements

The package does not provide or download data. Obtain the files from the PSID Data Center, under “Packaged Data” > “Main and Supplemental Studies” (https://simba.isr.umich.edu/Zips/ZipMain.aspx), where the Family Files and the Cross-year Individual file are listed. Access requires registering with the PSID and having authorization to download the files; the package never handles credentials. The package needs the Cross-year Individual file and the Family File of every survey year requested in the panel.

Workflow

  1. Import the PSID files with getPSID().
  2. Choose the variables (fam.vars and ind.vars).
  3. Build the panel with build.panel().
  4. Keep the rows you need (the panel is in long format).

Import

Place the downloaded zips in one folder and import them:

getPSID("path/to/downloaded-psid", "path/to/psid-output")

getPSID() imports the family and individual files as .rda files named FAM<year>ER.rda and IND<year>ER.rda in the output folder. getFamilyPSID() and getIndPSID() import a single prefix, and processPSID() is the underlying function, which also accepts folders or loose .txt and .sas pairs.

Choosing the variables

fam.vars takes Family File variables (“PSID Family-level”) and ind.vars Cross-year Individual variables (“PSID Individual-level”).

fam.vars and ind.vars are data.frames with an integer year column and one column per variable. Each cell holds the PSID variable name for that wave, and the column name becomes the variable name in the output. Do not use column names that contain year or variable (for example birth_year or my_variable): build.panel() stops with an error. ind.vars holds individual-file variables such as survey weights and must not include the identifier variables ER30001 and ER30002. The format is:

> head(i)  # individual file example
   year     age    educ empstat  weight
1: 1968 ER30004 ER30010    <NA> ER30019
2: 1969 ER30023    <NA>    <NA> ER30042        # NOTICE THE NA for educ HERE
3: 1970 ER30046 ER30052    <NA> ER30066
4: 1971 ER30070 ER30076    <NA> ER30090
5: 1972 ER30094 ER30100    <NA> ER30116
6: 1973 ER30120 ER30126    <NA> ER30137

> head(f)  # family file example
   year age_youngest_child debt empstat_ faminc hours hvalue ...
1: 1968               V120 <NA>     V196    V81   V47     V5 ...
2: 1969              V1013 <NA>     V639   V529  V465   V449 ...
3: 1970              V1243 <NA>    V1278  V1514 V1138  V1122 ...
4: 1971              V1946 <NA>    V1983  V2226 V1839  V1823 ...
5: 1972              V2546 <NA>    V2581  V2852 V2439  V2423 ...
6: 1973              V3099 <NA>    V3114  V3256 V3027  V3021 ...

A cell that is NA means the variable does not exist in that wave; the returned column is NA for that wave. ind.vars is optional. Find the names in the PSID Data Center Variable Search (https://simba.isr.umich.edu/DC/s.aspx), which searches name, label, question and explanation text and can be filtered by data type and year, and in the PSID codebooks.

build.panel() uses exactly the names given; the same concept has a different name in each wave (total family income is V81 in 1968 and V529 in 1969). The crosswalk psid.xlsx lists, for each variable, its name in every wave, and getNamesPSID() reads it: given the name in any wave, including a wave you do not request, it returns the names in the others. It gives names, not definitions; check the codebook for changes of definition between waves. A variable with the same name in every wave (for example ER32000, sex of the individual) is repeated in every row.

cwf <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(system.file("psid-lists", "psid.xlsx", package = "localpsidR"))
getNamesPSID("ER17013", cwf, years = c(2003, 2005, 2007))

To build fam.vars from one name per variable, look the name up with getNamesPSID(). It returns the year as text such as "Y2003", and years must be given in ascending order (otherwise the names are paired with the wrong years):

yrs <- c(2019, 2021, 2023)
get_names <- function(x) getNamesPSID(x, cwf, years = yrs)$variable
fam.vars <- data.frame(year   = yrs,
                       faminc = get_names("ER71426"),
                       hours  = get_names("ER71233"))

Or write the tables by hand and build the panel:

fam.vars <- data.frame(year = c(1968, 1969), faminc = c("V81", "V529"), hours = c("V47", "V465"))
ind.vars <- data.frame(year = c(1968, 1969), age = c("ER30004", "ER30023"), weight = c("ER30019", "ER30042"))
build.panel(datadir = "path/to/psid-output", fam.vars = fam.vars, ind.vars = ind.vars,
            design = "all")

The result always contains ID1968, pernum, interview, sequence, relation.head, pid and year, plus one column per requested variable. The order of the columns of fam.vars matters: in each wave build.panel() takes the first family variable that has a name in that wave and drops the rows where it is NA (families that did not respond). Put first a variable that is filled for every responding family in every wave, such as the number of people in the family unit.

Building the panel

build.panel() reads the FAM<year>ER and IND<year>ER files from a data directory and returns a long-format data.table (one row per person and wave) with a pid column (the person identifier, constructed from ID1968 and pernum) and a year column, plus the requested variables.

build.panel(datadir = "path/to/psid-output",
            fam.vars = fam.vars,
            ind.vars = ind.vars)

The merge matches the interview number of each family file to the interview number of the same year in the individual file. fam.vars supplies the substantive variables and ind.vars the person-level variables.

heads.only = TRUE keeps heads only (relation.head equal to the head code and sequence 1 to 20; in 1968, which has no sequence number, the head code alone). current.heads.only = TRUE keeps current heads only (relation.head equal to the head code and sequence 1; in 1968, the head code alone). sample selects a sample ("SRC", "SEO", "immigrant" or "latino"; NULL does no subsetting). design controls which individuals are kept: "balanced" keeps individuals present in every requested wave, "all" keeps everyone, and an integer keeps individuals present in at least that many consecutive waves.

For example, heads of the SRC sample only:

build.panel(datadir = "~/psid", fam.vars = f, ind.vars = i,
            heads.only = TRUE, sample = "SRC", design = "all")

Long format: which rows to keep

The sequence column describes the status of the person at the interview of that wave (PSID individual codebook, verified on real data for waves 2011 to 2023): 1 to 20, in the family at the time of the interview; 51 to 59, in an institution; 71 to 80, moved out of the family and established an own household since the previous wave; 81 to 89, died since the previous wave; 0, born or moved in after the interview. Persons with sequence equal to 0 carry the family interview number of that wave but have relation.head equal to 0 and no individual information.

Which rows to keep. Members of the family at the time of the interview: sequence from 1 to 20. Current heads (reference persons): relation.head equal to 10 together with sequence equal to 1; code 10 alone also includes heads of the previous wave who died, are in an institution or moved out. Spouses or partners: relation.head equal to 20 or 22 among the members. On real data for waves 2011 to 2023, all member rows (sequence 1 to 20) with these codes have sequence 2.

Family-file variables are repeated on every row of the family. For analyses at the family level keep one row per family, that is the head (code 10 and sequence 1); otherwise a family is counted once per member.

For the waves 2011 to 2023, the number of rows with sequence 1 to 20 per wave and the number of heads with sequence 1 per wave equal the figures in the PSID individual codebook (number of persons in the family and number of families interviewed). For earlier waves the user should check the codebook.

d <- build.panel(datadir = "path/to/psid-output",
                 fam.vars = fam.vars,
                 ind.vars = ind.vars,
                 heads.only = FALSE,
                 current.heads.only = FALSE,
                 design = "all")

# keep family members
d[d$sequence >= 1 & d$sequence <= 20, ]

# keep current heads
d[d$relation.head == 10 & d$sequence == 1, ]

# keep spouses or partners
d[d$sequence >= 1 & d$sequence <= 20 & d$relation.head %in% c(20, 22), ]

# keep heads and spouses together
d[d$sequence >= 1 & d$sequence <= 20 &
    (d$relation.head == 10 & d$sequence == 1 |
       d$relation.head %in% c(20, 22)), ]

heads.only and current.heads.only keep heads only (see “Building the panel”). To keep heads and spouses together, set both to FALSE and use the filter above.

Variable lists and the crosswalk

The package ships variable lists (inst/psid-lists/famvars.txt and indvars.txt). The crosswalk psid.xlsx and cwf are defined in “Choosing the variables”.

extendVarsPSID() extends a variable list to waves that are missing from it, using the crosswalk:

f <- data.table::fread(system.file("psid-lists", "famvars.txt", package = "localpsidR"), na.strings = "")
ext <- extendVarsPSID(f, cwf)
ext$review  # inspect: every line that is not "added"

Check ext$review against the PSID codebooks before using the result, because a variable can change definition between waves even when its crosswalk name changes consistently. The crosswalk can be your own newer psid.xlsx — for example one with corrected variable names for waves this package already supports. Waves later than the latest one this package supports also need a package update, because build.panel() stops for unsupported waves even when the lists have been extended.

New waves

getPSID() detects the variable names of waves that are not built in and writes them to psid_waves_detected.csv (variable names and years only, no respondent data) in the output folder. Import both the IND and the FAM zip, then build with detect_waves = TRUE:

getPSID(inputdir = "path/to/downloaded-psid", outputdir = "path/to/psid-output")
build.panel(datadir = "path/to/psid-output",
            fam.vars = data.frame(year = <year>, v = "<variable name>"),
            detect_waves = TRUE, head_code = <head code>)

datadir must contain psid_waves_detected.csv. build.panel() logs a warning listing the variable names it uses. The head code is head_code if given, otherwise it is carried over from the latest built-in wave with a warning (head_code is ignored unless detect_waves = TRUE). For each detected year, build.panel() stops if fewer than 80% of the nonzero individual interview numbers appear among the family interview numbers. Only the modern family-interview label form (<YYYY> FAMILY INTERVIEW (ID) NUMBER) is detected. Detection is a convenience for a first look: verify the detected variable names and the head code against the PSID codebook, and make the wave permanent by editing makeids() (see ADDING_A_WAVE.md).

Differences from the original

This repository is a fork of psidR by Florian Oswald. The original authors keep full credit; the package is licensed under GPL-3.

  • Fixed the deprecated data.table with = FALSE syntax, which broke build.panel() when a requested family variable was NA.
  • Replaced the interactive download with local import (getPSID(), getFamilyPSID(), getIndPSID(), processPSID()); the package no longer downloads data or handles credentials.
  • Added support for the PSID 2023 wave and a wave framework.
  • Added extendVarsPSID() and data-raw/update-varlists.R to extend the variable lists to new waves.
  • Added detection of new waves (detect_waves, head_code, psid_waves_detected.csv).
  • Renamed the package to localpsidR.

Citation

citation("localpsidR") returns the original psidR reference first and the localpsidR reference second:

citation("localpsidR")

Please cite the original psidR package. If you also use the adaptations added by localpsidR, cite localpsidR as well.

The original package’s reference is kept as it is:

To cite the 'psidR' package in publications use:

  Florian Oswald (2021). psidR: Build Panel Data Sets from PSID Raw Data.
  R package version 2.1.

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Manual{,
    title = {psidR: Build Panel Data Sets from PSID Raw Data},
    author = {Florian Oswald},
    year = {2021},
    note = {R package version 2.1},
    url = {https://github.com/floswald/psidR},
  }

The original package’s Zenodo record is https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/9247059.
